# Experiments

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Plain-Language Summary
This section traces the experimental arc in two parts. The first part is the
**development history** on our original benchmark, which led us to a clean —
but, it turned out, **false** — story about architecture and backbones. The
second part documents the discovery that the benchmark was *leaking the
diagnostic answer into the note text*, and the **de-leaked re-evaluation**
that overturned several of our central conclusions, including which model
backbone is best.
:::

---

## Experimental Design Principles {#sec-exp-design}

All experiments share the following design constraints to ensure valid
comparison:

- **Same gold dataset** — experiments use the billable gold layer derived
  from MedSynth FY2026, in two versions: the original ("leaky") gold and the
  de-leaked gold in which diagnostic descriptions are removed from the note
  text (see the dataset section).
- **Content-addressed splits** — the de-leaked experiments use a split keyed
  by record id (sorted before partitioning), so the test partition is
  reproducible and identical across every de-leaked model. This makes the
  backbone comparison exact.
- **Same test set within a regime** — all de-leaked models are evaluated on
  the same 966-record held-out test set.
- **Logged provenance** — every run is logged with full parameter records.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two regimes, not directly comparable
Numbers in the **development history** below were measured on the *leaky*
benchmark and are not valid estimates of real performance. Numbers in the
**de-leaked re-evaluation** are the corrected results. We label every figure
with its regime; never compare a leaky number to a de-leaked one as if they
were the same quantity.
:::

---

## Understanding the Evaluation Metrics {#sec-exp-metrics}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Plain-Language Summary
Before the results, this section explains what the evaluation metrics measure
and why we chose them — particularly important for a 1,926-class problem where
the choice of averaging method changes what the number means.
:::

---

### Top-1 Accuracy

The simplest metric: of all test records, what fraction did the model predict
correctly?

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{Correct predictions}}{\text{Total predictions}} = \frac{743}{966} = 76.9\%$$

(using the de-leaked best model, E-024, as the worked example.)

**What it tells you:** How often the system gets the right answer.

**What it conceals:** Whether errors are evenly distributed across all 1,926
codes, or concentrated in a small number of difficult ones.

In multi-class classification, accuracy is equivalent to the **micro F1
score** — it pools all predictions together. A model that perfectly predicts
the 100 most common codes and fails on the remaining 1,826 could still achieve
high accuracy if the common codes dominate the test set.

In our case the test set is **uniform** (approximately 5 records per code), so
accuracy is a fair metric here. On real clinical data — where hypertension,
diabetes, and back pain dominate — it would be dangerously misleading.

---

### F1 Score: The Building Block

**F1 score** for a single class is the harmonic mean of precision and recall:

$$F1 = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

Where precision and recall are computed using a **One-vs-Rest** approach —
each class is treated as a binary classification problem in turn:

- **Precision** — of all the times the model predicted this code, how often
  was it correct? A high-precision model avoids false alarms.
- **Recall** — of all the records that truly had this code, how many did the
  model find? A high-recall model avoids missed detections.

For a concrete example using `I10` (Essential hypertension):

| | Predicted I10 | Predicted other |
|---|---|---|
| **True I10** | 5 TP | 1 FN |
| **True other** | 0 FP | 960 TN |

$$\text{Precision}_{I10} = \frac{5}{5+0} = 1.00 \qquad
  \text{Recall}_{I10} = \frac{5}{5+1} = 0.833 \qquad
  F1_{I10} = 0.909$$

This per-class F1 is computed separately for all 1,926 codes. The question is
then: how do we average 1,926 F1 scores into a single number?

---

### Three Averaging Strategies — and Why They Give Different Answers

**Macro average** computes the simple unweighted mean across all classes —
every class counts equally regardless of how many examples it has:

$$\text{Macro F1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} F1_i$$

**Weighted average** weights each class by its number of examples (its
*support*):

$$\text{Weighted F1} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\text{support}_i}{\text{total}} \times F1_i$$

**Micro average** pools all True Positives, False Positives, and False
Negatives across all classes before computing F1. For single-label
classification this is mathematically identical to accuracy.

| Averaging | Treats classes | Best when |
|---|---|---|
| **Macro** | Equally | All classes matter equally regardless of frequency |
| **Weighted** | Proportionally to frequency | Common classes matter more |
| **Micro** | By prediction volume | Only overall throughput matters |

---

### Why This Project Uses Macro F1

**Macro F1 is the right choice here for two reasons.**

First, **all 1,926 ICD-10 codes are clinically equally important.** A rare
code for a serious condition — say `A06.1` (chronic intestinal amoebiasis) —
is no less significant than a common code for a routine condition like
`M25.562` (pain in left knee). Macro averaging encodes this equal importance
directly.

Second, **the training set is deliberately uniform** (~5 records per code), so
weighted averaging would converge toward macro averaging anyway; using macro
explicitly makes the equal-weight intention transparent.

::: {.callout-important}
## Macro F1 vs Accuracy: Why They Tell Different Stories

For this project both metrics are consistent because the test set is uniform.
On real clinical data they would diverge significantly. Consider a model that
masters the 50 most common ICD-10 codes (roughly 60% of real encounters) but
fails on the remaining 1,876:

- **Accuracy** (= Micro F1): ~60% — looks acceptable
- **Macro F1**: ~0.03 — catastrophically poor

Macro F1 exposes the failure that accuracy hides. This is why Macro F1 is the
primary metric for any automated coding system evaluated for clinical
deployment.
:::

**What Macro F1 = 0.672 means in practice** (de-leaked E-024): averaged equally
across all 1,926 codes, the best de-leaked model achieves an F1 of 0.672. This
is a solid result for a 1,926-class problem with ~4 training examples per
class; random guessing would produce a Macro F1 near zero.

---

### Expected Calibration Error (ECE)

ECE measures whether the model's confidence scores are trustworthy. A
perfectly calibrated model that says "70% confident" is correct exactly 70% of
the time.

$$\text{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{|B_b|}{n} \left| \text{acc}(B_b) - \text{conf}(B_b) \right|$$

| ECE | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| < 0.05 | Excellent — confidence scores are reliable |
| 0.05 – 0.15 | Good — minor overconfidence |
| 0.15 – 0.30 | Moderate — needs treatment |
| > 0.30 | Poor — confidence scores not meaningful |

The de-leaked best model (E-024) achieves **ECE = 0.039** after temperature
scaling — excellent calibration that makes the confidence threshold
operationally meaningful.

---

### Coverage@τ and Accuracy on Covered

These two metrics jointly describe the **selective automation** capability:

- **Coverage@τ** — the fraction of test records where the model's top-1
  confidence exceeds τ. For de-leaked E-024 at τ = 0.7: 73.7% of records are
  auto-coded.
- **Accuracy on covered** — the precision on the auto-coded subset. For E-024
  at τ = 0.7: 90.0% of auto-coded predictions are correct.

Together they define the operating point — see @sec-results-automation for the
full threshold sweep.

---

# Part I — Development History (leaky benchmark)

::: {.callout-warning}
## These results were measured on the leaky benchmark
The experiments in Part I were run before we discovered description leakage.
Their accuracy numbers are inflated and are **not** valid performance
estimates. We retain the two experiments whose lessons concern the *training
recipe* (warm initialisation), because those lessons survived de-leaking. The
leaky backbone and SupCon conclusions are documented in Part III, where the
de-leaked re-evaluation overturns them.
:::

## E-003: Hierarchical Cold Start (leaky regime) {#sec-exp-e003}

**Hypothesis:** The hierarchical two-stage architecture works even without
special initialisation.

**Setup:** Stage-1 router from E-001 weights; Stage-2 resolvers trained from
base Bio_ClinicalBERT (cold start — no ICD-10 pre-training).

| Metric (leaky regime) | Value |
|---|---|
| Stage-1 accuracy | 96.4% |
| Stage-2 within-chapter | 11.7% |
| E2E accuracy | 11.1% |

: E-003 results (leaky regime). {#tbl-exp-e003}

**Interpretation (survives de-leaking):** The architecture collapses without
warm initialisation. Despite near-perfect chapter routing, the within-chapter
resolvers cannot learn from ~4 examples per code starting from a general-domain
model. This lesson is about the *training recipe*, not the leaked signal, and
holds independent of leakage: Stage-2 must be warm-started.

::: {.callout-important}
## The Cold Start Problem
With ~4 training examples per code and up to 263 codes per chapter, a Stage-2
resolver trained from scratch has insufficient gradient signal to discriminate
codes it has no prior representation of. Warm-starting from a flat ICD-10
classifier — an encoder that has already learned to distinguish codes — is what
makes the architecture viable. This conclusion is unaffected by the leakage
issue, since it concerns a catastrophic failure mode (≈11% E2E) far below any
level leakage could explain away.
:::

## E-009 → E-010: Warm Initialisation Worked (leaky regime) {#sec-exp-e009}

**Hypothesis:** Initialising Stage-2 resolvers from a flat ICD-10 classifier
(E-002) dramatically improves within-chapter accuracy; deeper flat
pre-training helps further.

**Result (leaky regime):** Warm initialisation lifted E2E from the cold-start
~11% to ~80% (E-009, 20-epoch init) and ~86% (E-010, 40-epoch init). The
*qualitative* lesson — warm-start is necessary and beneficial — is robust. The
*specific* magnitudes are leaky-regime and are superseded by Part III; we do
not treat the 85.8% figure as a valid result.

::: {.callout-note}
## What survives, and what does not
**Survives:** the architecture needs a warm-started Stage-2 (E-003 vs E-009).
**Superseded:** the headline accuracy (85.8%) and any conclusion drawn from
comparing leaky configurations — including the backbone ranking and the SupCon
result, both overturned in Part III.
:::

---

# Part II — The Leakage Discovery {#sec-exp-leakage}

After establishing the leaky-regime results above, an audit of the gold data
revealed that the certified redaction which produced it had stripped ICD-10
*codes* from the note text but **left the human-readable code *descriptions* in
place**. For example, a note assigned `M25.562` still contained the phrase
"pain in left knee" — the literal description of that code — in its assessment
text.

This let the model **read the answer rather than infer it**: the Stage-2
resolver could match a description phrase to a code without performing any
clinical reasoning. Because the descriptions are near-verbatim restatements of
the code definitions, this is answer leakage, not legitimate signal.

A deterministic redactor (v5) was built to remove the descriptions, producing
the **de-leaked gold**. A residual ~18.6% of records retain some partial
description overlap that the redactor could not safely remove, so the de-leaked
numbers, if anything, *slightly over-estimate* a perfectly clean ceiling.

Every conclusion that depended on within-chapter code resolution had to be
re-evaluated, because that is exactly where the leaked signal operated.

---

# Part III — De-leaked Re-evaluation {#sec-exp-deleaked}

All experiments below use the de-leaked gold and the content-addressed split
(identical 966-record test set across models).

## E-021: ClinicalBERT, De-leaked {#sec-exp-e021}

**Setup:** The E-010 recipe (hierarchical, warm-started ClinicalBERT
resolvers) retrained and evaluated on de-leaked gold.

| Metric (de-leaked) | Value | vs leaky (E-010) |
|---|---|---|
| E2E accuracy | 59.2% | was 85.8% |
| Macro F1 | 0.477 | was 0.762 |
| Stage-1 accuracy | 95.6% | was 96.9% |
| Within-chapter | 62.0% | was 84.8% |
| ECE | 0.088 | was 0.031 |
| Coverage@0.7 | 55.3% | was 86.4% |

: E-021 — ClinicalBERT de-leaked. {#tbl-exp-e021}

**Interpretation:** Removing description leakage drops ClinicalBERT's E2E by
25.7 points (~30% relative). Stage-1 routing barely changes (96.9%→95.6%) —
the inflation was almost entirely in within-chapter resolution (84.8%→62.0%),
exactly where the leaked descriptions were exploitable. This is the corrected
headline for the original backbone.

## E-024: Clinical ModernBERT, De-leaked — the New Best {#sec-exp-e024}

**Hypothesis (revisited):** On the leaky benchmark, Clinical ModernBERT had
appeared to lose badly to ClinicalBERT (48.8% vs 85.8%). Does that ranking
hold once the leaked signal — which an older model might exploit differently —
is removed?

**Setup:** Identical de-leaked pipeline and test set to E-021; only the
backbone changes (`Simonlee711/Clinical_ModernBERT`). For fairness the
ClinicalBERT recipe is matched exactly, including `max_length=512` (not
ModernBERT-optimal, but identical to the comparison model).

| Metric (de-leaked) | E-024 ModernBERT | E-021 ClinicalBERT |
|---|---|---|
| E2E accuracy | **76.9%** | 59.2% |
| Macro F1 | **0.672** | 0.477 |
| Stage-1 accuracy | 95.3% | 95.6% |
| Within-chapter | **80.7%** | 62.0% |
| ECE | **0.039** | 0.088 |
| Coverage@0.7 | **73.7%** | 55.3% |

: E-024 vs E-021 — the backbone ranking inverts. {#tbl-exp-e024}

**Interpretation — the central result:** De-leaked, Clinical ModernBERT beats
ClinicalBERT by ~18 points E2E, *reversing* the leaky-benchmark ranking. The
two routers are near-identical (95.3% vs 95.6%), so the entire difference is in
within-chapter resolution (80.7% vs 62.0%). The advantage is broad: ModernBERT
wins 17 of 19 chapters (see @sec-results-chapter), which rules out a localised
residual-leak artifact and points to a genuinely stronger backbone.

::: {.callout-important}
## A leaky benchmark ranked the backbones backwards
The leaky data did not merely inflate scores — it inverted a conclusion. The
strong description signal was best exploited by the older ClinicalBERT, making
it appear superior. Once the leak is removed, the more modern architecture's
genuine advantage emerges across nearly the entire code space. The original
paper's "ClinicalBERT is the right backbone" conclusion was an artifact of the
leak.
:::

## E-026: BioClinical ModernBERT, De-leaked {#sec-exp-e026}

**Setup:** Same de-leaked pipeline; backbone
`thomas-sounack/BioClinical-ModernBERT-base`.

| Metric (de-leaked) | E-026 | vs leaky (E-013) |
|---|---|---|
| E2E accuracy | 39.8% | was 7.0% |
| Macro F1 | 0.289 | was 0.046 |
| ECE | 0.049 | was 0.013 |
| Coverage@0.7 | 18.3% | was 1.7% |

: E-026 — BioClinical ModernBERT de-leaked. {#tbl-exp-e026}

**Interpretation:** BioClinical ModernBERT remains the weakest of the three
backbones, but is far from the "catastrophic failure" (7.0%) the leaky run
suggested — its leaky number was depressed, not inflated, an asymmetry we do
not fully explain. The clear ordering on de-leaked data is **Clinical
ModernBERT (76.9%) > ClinicalBERT (59.2%) > BioClinical ModernBERT (39.8%)**:
architecture family alone does not determine performance; the specific
pretraining does.

## E-022: SupCon on the Z Chapter, De-leaked {#sec-exp-e022}

**Hypothesis (revisited):** On the leaky benchmark, Supervised Contrastive
fine-tuning of the Z resolver appeared to lift Z accuracy by +21.2pp and was
described as "solving" the Z chapter. How much of that survives de-leaking?

**Setup:** The E-014 two-phase SupCon procedure (contrastive fine-tune then
head refit) applied to the de-leaked ClinicalBERT Z resolver, evaluated in a
hybrid system (E-021 for all non-Z chapters, SupCon Z for chapter Z).

| Metric (de-leaked) | Value | Leaky claim |
|---|---|---|
| Z resolver validation accuracy | 0.614 → 0.674 (+6.1pp) | "62.1% → 83.3% (+21.2pp)" |
| Hybrid system E2E | 0.592 → 0.597 (+0.5pp) | "85.8% → 86.7% (+0.9pp)" |

: E-022 — SupCon Z de-leaked. {#tbl-exp-e022}

**Interpretation:** The dramatic leaky Z gain was overwhelmingly a leakage
artifact. De-leaked, SupCon produces a modest genuine improvement on the Z
resolver's validation accuracy (~6pp) that nearly vanishes at the system level
(+0.5pp). The effect is small enough to be sensitive to the data partition. The
claim that SupCon "solves the Z chapter" does not hold; the honest statement is
that contrastive learning gives a small, real, but system-negligible
improvement that the leaky benchmark overstated by roughly an order of
magnitude.

## MIMIC-IV Real-World Validation (De-leaked Model) {#sec-exp-mimic}

**Purpose:** Quantify the synthetic-to-real gap by evaluating the de-leaked
ClinicalBERT model (E-021) on 4,877 real MIMIC-IV discharge summaries.

| Metric | MedSynth (de-leaked) | MIMIC-IV (real) |
|---|---|---|
| E2E Accuracy | 59.2% | **8.1%** |
| Macro F1 | 0.477 | 0.042 |
| ECE | 0.088 | 0.318 |
| Coverage@0.7 | 55.3% | 20.2% |

: MIMIC-IV validation, de-leaked model. {#tbl-mimic}

**Interpretation:** On real notes the de-leaked system scores 8.1% E2E (the
leaky model had scored 12.0%). Both collapse to near-floor, so the
synthetic-to-real gap is driven by **domain shift** and is largely independent
of leakage. Real discharge summaries use abbreviations, shorthand, copy-paste
artefacts, and institution-specific terminology absent from the synthetic
training data.

::: {.callout-note}
## A caveat specific to the de-leaked real-world number
The de-leaked model was trained on description-redacted notes, but real MIMIC
notes still contain descriptions. This train/serve asymmetry means the de-leaked
8.1% is not a perfectly clean estimate of real-world capability; a fully fair
measurement requires inference-time parity between training and serving text.
Either way, both regimes land near the floor — the dominant problem is domain
shift, not the precise leakage treatment.
:::

## Experiment Summary {#sec-exp-summary}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-exp-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Experiment progression. Part I is leaky-regime development history; Part III is the de-leaked re-evaluation used for all reported results."

import pandas as pd

experiments = [
    {"ID": "E-003", "Regime": "leaky (history)", "Description": "Hierarchical cold start",
     "E2E Acc": "11.1%", "Note": "Shows warm-init is required (lesson survives)"},
    {"ID": "E-009/010", "Regime": "leaky (history)", "Description": "Warm-started ClinicalBERT",
     "E2E Acc": "~80–86%", "Note": "Leaky — superseded by E-021"},
    {"ID": "**E-021**", "Regime": "de-leaked", "Description": "ClinicalBERT (hier)",
     "E2E Acc": "59.2%", "Note": "Corrected headline for original backbone"},
    {"ID": "**E-024**", "Regime": "de-leaked", "Description": "Clinical ModernBERT",
     "E2E Acc": "**76.9%**", "Note": "**De-leaked BEST — ranking inverted**"},
    {"ID": "E-026", "Regime": "de-leaked", "Description": "BioClinical ModernBERT",
     "E2E Acc": "39.8%", "Note": "Weakest backbone"},
    {"ID": "E-022", "Regime": "de-leaked", "Description": "ClinicalBERT + SupCon Z",
     "E2E Acc": "59.7%", "Note": "SupCon +0.5pp (leaky claim was +21.2pp on Z)"},
    {"ID": "MIMIC-IV", "Regime": "de-leaked", "Description": "Real-world (E-021)",
     "E2E Acc": "8.1%", "Note": "Domain shift dominates"},
]

df = pd.DataFrame(experiments)
from IPython.display import Markdown
display(Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False)))
```

### Key Findings

**Finding 1: The architecture requires warm initialisation (survives
de-leaking).** Cold-start (E-003, 11.1%) collapses; warm-starting Stage-2 from
a flat ICD-10 classifier is necessary for the hierarchical design to work. This
lesson concerns the training recipe and is independent of the leakage issue.

**Finding 2: Description leakage inflated the headline by ~30% relative.**
ClinicalBERT's hierarchical E2E falls from a reported 85.8% (leaky) to 59.2%
(de-leaked, E-021), almost entirely in within-chapter resolution.

**Finding 3: Leakage inverted the backbone ranking — the central result.** On
clean data, Clinical ModernBERT (E-024, 76.9%) beats ClinicalBERT (E-021,
59.2%) by ~18 points, winning 17 of 19 chapters — the reverse of the leaky
benchmark, on which we had wrongly concluded "domain pretraining beats
architectural modernity." A leaky benchmark ranked the backbones backwards.

**Finding 4: The "SupCon solves the Z chapter" result was an artifact.** The
leaky +21.2pp Z gain becomes +0.5pp at the system level once de-leaked (E-022).
Contrastive learning gives a small genuine effect that the leak overstated by
roughly an order of magnitude.

**Finding 5: Neither model generalises to real notes.** On 4,877 MIMIC-IV
discharge summaries the de-leaked system scores 8.1% E2E (leaky model: 12.0%).
The synthetic-to-real gap is domain-shift driven and largely independent of
leakage.

**Overarching contribution:** A leaky synthetic benchmark did not merely
inflate scores — it inverted an architectural conclusion and manufactured an
apparent algorithmic win (SupCon) that does not exist. This is a cautionary
result for the evaluation of clinical-NLP systems on synthetic data.
